Scotch Corner Gateway

Scotch Corner Gateway The "Scotch Corner" Gateway Key: 1 Time switch 2 Mobile phone in hands-free kit for monitoring audio 3 Yaesu FT2600 2m tcvr 4 Home brew interface 5 Switch mode PSU 6 ISDN terminal adaptor 7 PC - 233 MHz Pentium 8 BT Easyreach pager for emergency shutdown 9 VHF / UHF diplexor 10 70cm TX / Rx (Yes; we do have wallpaper at this QTH - but the gateway is in the loft to keep the xyl happy! ) NoV Holders: G4FZN & G8HQW & 2E1GUN Transmit: 14dBw erp Maximum Deviation: +/- 2.5kHz Antenna: Omnidirectional (vertical polarization) Frequencies: 145.3375MHz & 431.200MHz Identification: Morse Code, 22wpm Audio frequency 459Hz Coverage map of the Scotch Corner Gateway (100kB) The Scotch Corner Gateway operates on 145.3375MHz. eQSO software is usually operated. No repeater shift is required, and no access tones are needed. The gateway operates a simple squelch system, which means any signal on the frequency will be accepted. In the future, if more internet gateways become operational, and QRM becomes more of a problem, the Scotch Corner Gateway may have to resort to CTCSS tone squelch. Chris, G4FZN will resist this for as long as possible! Incoming signals are re-radiated on 431.200MHz when the gateway is in operation. (see below) Being a simplex system, the gateway cannot relay signals from one radio user in the North East to another radio user in the North East. Most stations in this area are able to hear the other users direct, but there are times when the gateway can hear two stations who can't hear each other. In this situation, a repeater could assist communications BUT a simplex gateway can not help matters. Why is this? Because, unlike a duplex repeater with a frequency split, a simplex gateway cannot transmit and receive at the same time. For this reason, the 70cms frequency (431.200MHz) has been added recently. The output power on 431.200MHz is very low - 3 watts erp - however the audio from the internet is mixed with audio from the two metre receiver and retransmitted on 431.200. At the time of writing, no 70cm receive frequency is available. Hours of Operation During weekdays, the Scotch Corner gateway is active from 7am to 10am, and from 4pm through to midnight. At weekends, operation if from 7am through to 1am without a gap. The RSGB news, read by Jeremy Boot, G4NJH, is transmitted at 10.30am on Sunday mornings. Alternatively, you can click here to listen now in Real Audio. Who is welcome to use it? All licenced amateurs are very welcome to use the gateway. Please bear in mind that after an over, there may be a delay of up to 20secs before the other station replies, and remember that the software is not yet finalized, and subject to continuous improvement. Who has to used it? In the future, if more internet gateways become operational, and QRM becomes more of a problem, the Scotch Corner Gateway may have to resort to CTCSS tone squelch. Chris, G4FZN will resist this for as long as possible! Being a simplex system, the gateway cannot relay signals from one radio user in the North East to another radio user in the North East. Most stations in this area are able to hear the other users direct, but there are times when the gateway can hear two stations who can't hear each other. In this situation, a repeater could assist communications BUT a simplex gateway can not help matters. Why is this? Because, unlike a duplex repeater with a frequency split, a simplex gateway cannot transmit and receive at the same time. For this reason, the 70cms frequency (431.200MHz) has been added recently. The output power on 431.200MHz is very low - 3 watts erp - however the audio from the internet is mixed with audio from the two metre receiver and retransmitted on 431.200. At the time of writing, no 70cm receive frequency is available. Who is welcome to use it? All licenced amateurs are very welcome to use the gateway. Please bear in mind that after an over, there may be a delay before the other station replies, and remember that the software is not yet finalized, and subject to continuous improvement. When the interference is occurring, it consists of very sharp strong clicks on the received signal. If enough of these clicks happen, then the squelch closes, and the incoming signal is lost. There is a clear distinction to be heard between a weak signal - such as one might easily obtain by using a Slim Jim - , and a signal suffering due to the repeater's interference. The difference is in the sound of the background noise. The normally weak signal has a constant "hash" behind it, whereas an interfered signal has a characteristic "crackle". For the interference to manifest, the repeater must also be transmitting. It is not caused by blocking of the receiver (ie. desense) - as blocking causes gaussian noise, not the prickly noise which is heard. However, the effect is similar to that of desense insofar as a station can bring the repeater with a tone burst, but as soon as the repeater keys up, the incoming signal disappears, and the repeater shuts down immediately. ( A continuous transmission of 8 seconds is required to "latch" it on ). GPS Page 31st January 1999 What is GPS ? The Global Positioning System (GPS) consists of 24 satellites in different orbits, each of which takes 12 hours to circle the earth. These satellites transmit information to earth, and can be received by members of the public - without any subscription needed - on a small GPS receiver. A GPS receiver requires visibility of at least three satellites, in order to compute its exact position on the earth's surface. For a three-dimensional fix, four satellites are required. Usually, there are between six and nine satellites "monitored" by the receiver. The writer owns a GPS II+. As happens, no sooner had I purchased this unti, that Garmin introduced a GPS III, which contains a complete road map of the UK. I have also seen a GPS III "pilot", which is an air based version of the GPS III, and it contains information useful to pilots, such as controlled air space charts, frequencies and air corridors. The GPS market is dominated by two companies, Garmin and Magellan. I have only experience of the Garmin products. If you have a Garmin GPS unit, it is well worth looking on the Garmin web site for updates to the software. My GPS II+ kept switching itself off for no apparent reason (Version 2.04 software), and I found an upgrade. The software is quite easy to upgrade, and full instructions are on the site. I am now running software version 2.07, and the unit no longer switches itself off! Waypoints To plot a course between two points (assuming they are less than a couple of hundred miles apart), you only need the start point, and the end point. Start up the engine, and away you go. However, in real-life, most courses are not as simple as that. At sea, you may wish to navigate around an island (!) or on land, you are forced into following public highways. So a course from A to B may well not be in a straight line. You need to set up a route. To do this, a number of points are chosen - called WAYPOINTS - which are then strung together in a fixed order, and - Hey presto - your route is again defined. Most GPS receivers can be programmed with waypoints. The GPS II+ can hold 500 of them, whereas other models can store 250 or less. Waypoints need not be points along a route, however, they are also used to mark reference points. I use waypoints to mark the location of amateur radio repeater stations, for example. As you move from one area to another, the GPS receiver can display the nearest "waypoints" (repeaters), and you always know which channel(s) to listen on for traffic reports. Waypoint files can be created, and uploaded into a GPS receiver using serial ASCII data and a suitable comms package. I use a program written by Garmin, called PCX5, however Procomm, or a similar communications program will do fine. Learning to manage this emotion can be rewarding. In the latter case, learning to express anger constructively will help you uncover other important emotions as well. Freeing anger will allow you to feel more energized. You may have trouble showing anger in appropriate ways because our society does not encourage such expressions. Suppressing anger is ultimately destructive to your well-being--it can even make you physically sick. Due to the connection between mind and body, disease and anger go hand in hand. Truly happy people have far fewer diseases than unhappy people. Therefore, you need to think about the ways that your anger affects you physically. AntiAging Skin sagging and wrinkling can be a sign of too much time spent on the beach or just a visible reminder of the relentless aging process. Cutaneous aging is a complex process affecting various layers of skin. Cutaneous aging includes the effects of gravity, expression lines, sleep lines, hormoral changes and genetic programming, and wind, smoke and chemical exposures. Innate or intrinsic aging, which affects skin by slow, irreversible degeneration of tissue. The consequences of innate aging can be observed over the entire surface of the body, including skin protected from the sun. As people age, innate or intrinsic aging changes their skin in ways that cause it to develop wrinkles. Few scientists had attributed skin aging to a single cause. But, recent research has revealed that a process long known to discolor and toughen food in storage also contributes to age-related changes in the skin. That process is primarily the chemical attachment of the sugar glucose to skin collagen without the aid of enzymes. When enzymes attach glucose to collagen, they do so for a specific purpose and at specific places. In contrast, the nonenzymatic process adds glucose haphazardly to any of several amino group sites along any available collagen molecule, as illustrated at the right (grey diamonds are glucose and black triangles are amino acids). The attachment of glucose to skin collagen triggers a series of spontaneous chemical reactions that culminate in the formation and eventual accumulation of irreversible cross-links between adjacent collagen molecules. The extensive cross-linking of collagen causes the loss of skin elasticity characteristic of aging. Therefore, "nonenzymatic glycosylation" of skin collagen is important, since it is the process that ages skin. The steps by which glucose alters skin collagen have been understood by food chemists for decades and only recently have biologists recognized that the same steps take place in the skin. The nonenzymatic glycosylation steps between glucose and collagen may seem complicated, but they are fairly straight forward compared with many biochemical reactions: A series of chemical reactions begin when an aldehyde group (CHO) of glucose and an amino group (NH 2 ) of a collagen molecule are attracted to each other. The glucose and amino group combine forming what is called a Schiff base. This combination is unstable and quickly rearranges itself into a stabler, but still reversible, substance known as an Amadori product. Long-lived collagen molecules persist in the body for years, allowing some of the Amadori products to slowly dehydrate and rearrange themselves yet again into new structures, called advanced glycosylation end-products (AGEs). AGEs are yellowish in color, and contribute to the yellowing of skin and age spots. AGEs are highly reactive, and in a final series of reactions, cross-link an adjacent collagen molecule. Windmills of Barbados Windmills of Barbados Glossary Within Barbados, windmills are described using a number of local terms. Where appropriate, to keep this report consistent with other documents, I have used the local terms, as follows: Barbados term British Term millwall windmill tower points sails roundhouse cap Survey of current millwalls - October 1999 Note on locations The names given to the location of millwalls in this list are largely of my own making, and may not be accurate. Sugar mills, by their very nature, were associated with plantations, and unless the mill and plantation house have survived together as an identifiable unit, it's not always obvious which plantation the mill went with. Coupling this with the vagueness of exact location that the Barbados maps tend to provide may mean that I have misidentified mills. Locations I am especially unsure or suspicious of I have identified with ?? Morgan Lewis Mill, St Andrew Morgan Lewis mill, commonly given the date c1727, continued to work through until 1945. In 1962 E L Banister donated it to the Barbados National Trust, who commenced a restoration project 2 years later. It was further restored in 1974, but deteriorated again, so much so that it was listed as one of the most endangered heritage sites in the world. However a 2 year restoration by the UK millwrights The Chiltern Partnership, started in 1996, has brought the mill back to its former glory. Coverley, Christ Church This unroofed millwall is in a reasonable state of repair, but does have a tree growing out of it. Graeme Hall, Christ Church In the grounds of a site owned by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development. The tower, now roofed and turretted, bears the date 1929 on the masonry of the turrets above a bell. The tower is of regular coral blocks, and shows signs of conversion from 1 large arch to 2 smaller ones. There is also a further tall, thin arch. Above the main doorway is another date, which reads B.R. 1703 (though the last digit is indistinct). Ealing Park, Christ Church This mill is now bordered by Millwall Avenue, part of the Ealing Park stage 3 development. The millwall itself is constructed of coral blocks, and is in the process of being incorporated into a house conversion. As is the case with much of the new building in Barbados, this conversion is taking its time, and there appears to have been little work for many months. Gibbons, Christ Church This 8 sided structure was considered by Prof Dash to have been an animal rather than a wind-mill. Golden Gate Park There are 2 traditional "Dutch style" windmills in Golden Gate Park, located at the western end to catch the ample sea breezes. The Dutch Windmill The Dutch Windmill was built in 1902, at a cost of $16,000, together with a Dutch Cottage alongside which was occupied by the mill's caretaker. 75 feet high, and 33 feet in diameter at the base, is sails had a span of 102 feet and meant it was capable of pumping 30,000 gallons of fresh water per hour from underground to a reservoir on Strawberry Hill. Despite being a great success for a few years (so much so that a second windmill was built), by 1913 electric pumps were introduced , so the windmills began to become obsolete. Much of the Dutch Mill's machinery was destroyed by a storm in the 1930's, followed by further gutting to aid the 2nd World War effort. In the winter of 1949 one of the sails was blown off, and a few months later the other 3 sails were removed for safety. A Citizens Commission formed in 1964 to start efforts to restore the mills, but despite receiving a Federal grant of $10,000 in 1968, it was not until August 1976 that volunteers from the US Navy Reserve started work on restoring the Dutch Mill . Work continued through to completion in 1981. Since then little additional work has been done, and although, as the many photos of the mill show, from the exterior the mill looks impressive, structurally it's showing signs of decay again . At the base of the mill, the grounds have been laid out as the Queen Wilhelmina Tulip Garden - a fact that contributes to the popularity of the mill as a photo location. It's also given rise to the often repeated, but false story that the mill "was a gift to the city of San Francisco from Holland"! Point to note: Looking at historical pictures of the mill, it's apparent that the "restored" mill's sails rotate in the opposite direction to the original sails! Circa 1940's hand coloured print Dutch Mill in 1999. The Murphy Windmill With the undoubted success of the Dutch Mill , in 1905 a second windmill was built to the south, known as the Murphy Windmill, after Samuel G Murphy who donated $20,000 (one source says $25,000) for its construction. This mill was even larger than the first, 95 feet high, with sails 114 feet across, capable of pumping 40,000 gallons per hour, and survived slightly longer before electric pumps were installed. Sadly this mill has never been restored, and currently stands sailless and neglected, slowly deteriorating. The Murphy Windmill has a concrete base, surmounted by a slate clad wooden upper body, and each year more slates fall from the mill. The remains of the sails are stacked in the undergrowth nearby. Not surprisingly, despite the many web sites with photos of the Dutch Mill , no-one seems to want to put up pictures of the forlorn Murphy windmill. As it was in 1999. Once you are sure you would like to apply, you can fill out the application. Here are the answers to some questions you may have. What will I do as a CL? Serve as an example to other homesteaders. This includes having good home pages that fit the Petsburgh theme with no content violations, and having a "developed" page. This means it should have at least two sub pages. Monitor specific blocks in your neighborhood (as specified by the Liaison). You'll be looking for great sites and those pages that don't meet the content guidelines, which you will tell Geocities about so they can contact the owners or remove them if necessary; and content that doesn't match the theme of the Petsburgh neighborhood. Act as a liaison between your neighbors and Geocities. Your member name and e-mail address will be posted in a prominent place within the neighborhood so everyone will know who to contact if they have questions or problems. We encourage members to think of you as their primary resource, for everything from HTML problems to content guidelines to neighborhood themes. Some leaders may get 10 and 20 messages a day, sometimes more and most of the time less. Keep your own home page fresh and lively. If we're holding you out as leaders of the community, your own site should be a showcase. It doesn't have to be completely whiz-bang (although your fellow Community Leaders may be able to help you spice it up), but it should be updated at least once a week. It absolutely MUST conform to Geocities content guidelines and to the theme of your neighborhood. If it doesn't, your application will be automatically rejected. Recruit and nominate new Community Leaders by referring those who you think qualify to the Community Leader Application. You will also be asked to vote on applicants. You will be responsible for communicating with your fellow community leaders via email regarding Petsburgh Business. Although not mandatory, your presence is encouraged at the Petsburgh CL meetings held weekly and will help us ensure that Petsburgh is running efficiently. In addition, please notify your Liaison when any change in your email, URL, or committee work occurs. Probably some other things we haven't thought of yet, but we'll let you know when we do. What are the requirements of being a CL? Be an established homesteader in the Petsburgh community. Good HTML knowledge. We will not be able to train you on HTML and you will be answering a lot of HTML questions. Familiar with GeoCities utilities. Complete compliance with the Content Guidelines. We strongly urge you to have the GeoGuide on at least your index.html page. Willingness to help. Good commun

From: Ferd - Petsburgh Park Co-Liaison Haah, I've read what some people have said about why they became CLs, and I wanted to present the male engineer point of view. I didn't go through a painful learning process. My background is architecture, engineering, and computer science. I started back when the Internet was still the Arpanet (well, actually, I started in the days of punch cards and teletypes). I ran a mailing list for 15 years, taught programming at the local community college, and *part* of my job has often including being the system administrator for everything from a supermini to a couple of dozen UN*X workstations. I wrote my first web page about 4 years ago. At the time, the only browser was Mosaic and we used HTML 1.0. I like HTML because it is a markup language like TeX (I'm a local TeXpert). One of my hobbies is learning new computer languages, which is one reason why I learned HTML, Perl, and Java. I've even written programs in PostScript; it's not just for printers. Given that background, I decided to become a CL so I could enlighten the masses. That's not meant to be a snobby comment -- I want to help people get over the initial hump in the learning curve. The more people who know how to write good HTML, the more good pages I'll see. I didn't join to meet people; I've had net friends from British Columbia, England, and Australia, and I already get more email than I want. That's why I joined the C&R Committee instead of the Welcome Committee. I don't get much steader email, which I think is mostly because of the block I run. While it contains a few really good sites, it's about 70% NMIYs (yes, I've sent a welcome letter to everyone). I have helped a few people get started, and one person graduated from using GeoBuilder to writing HTML. OTOH, most of the questions I get are from other areas of Petsburgh. They all write back to thank me for helping or to ask more questions. My favorite is the one where the steader thanked me for answering her question nicely instead of saying something nasty (she had misread some instructions). Yeah, maybe I should have a page in Silicon Valley, but I don't want a site about writing HTML. (Maybe someday ....) I started in Heartland because I wanted to create a site about our horses and cats, then I moved to Petsburgh a few days after it opened. Heck, the reason we bought our first horse was so I'd get outside more. I knew almost nothing about horses, and I didn't even know you lead them on the left! HTML, yes; horses, no :-) Since then I've learned to ride and have raised a couple of foals. Lemme sum up this way -- I want to help new steaders learn HTML and good web page design the same way other people have taught me about horses. Eleanor's room was modest, with pale blue walls adorned with various sports pennants. A wooden desk, worn at the edges, held a collection of mismatched pens and a faded calendar. The faint smell of lavender lingered in the air, mixed with the earthy scent of bookshelves lined with novels, half of them dog-eared from use. A small, well-loved chair, upholstered in soft plaid, sat beside a window where sunlight filtered through sheer curtains. The sense of belonging and shared experiences in her youth. I catch the faintest whiff of that lavender air freshener I used to love, and it pulls me back through time. My desk, though cluttered, holds pieces of who I was—faded notes from cheer practice and scrawled reminders about games. I can still hear the laughter of friends echoing from the soccer field, the excitement of the crowd cheering us on. Those were the days when the future felt so bright, when each moment was filled with possibility. I can close my eyes and recall the warmth of the sun on my skin, the vibrant colors of our uniforms, how they swayed with every cheer. Yet, there's an ache in my chest, a whisper of something that’s just out of reach. It’s as though all those memories have slipped through my fingers, like the remnants of an episode, the ones lost to time and only faintly remembered now.

Clara's living room is a modest space, with faded lilac wallpaper and a worn, floral-patterned sofa that has seen better days. A slender bookshelf leans slightly to one side, crammed with dog-eared novels and framed photographs. The air carries a faint scent of vanilla from a half-burned candle on the coffee table, mingling with the crispness of the late afternoon light filtering through lace curtains. Clara lost her infant son, Levi. I sit here, the sun casting soft patterns on the sofa, and I remember Levi's laughter, even though it was all too brief. Big brother used to tease him with silly faces, and I could hardly contain my joy as I watched them. I can still see his tiny hands, so perfectly formed, and how he would curl his fingers around mine. The world feels so heavy without him, each day a reminder of what should have been. My heart aches in the quiet moments, when the house is still and I can almost hear the whispers of his soft coos. The smell of vanilla lingers, an echo of my attempts to fill this space with warmth, yet I feel the emptiness all the more. Just yesterday, I picked up his blanket, and the softness reminded me of when I held him close, wrapped in love and hope. I wonder if he feels that warmth still, wherever he is.

Evelyn's room was modestly decorated, with soft, beige walls and a worn, floral armchair near the window. I catch glimpses of the afternoon sun spilling through the window, casting golden patches on the dusty floor. The lavender sachet still gives a gentle scent, reminding me of our afternoons spent in the garden. I can almost hear his laughter, echoing through the house during those warm summer days. He would have loved the way the light dances along the quilt that covers my bed, how it brightens the colors and makes everything feel alive. I wish he were here to tell me about the things that captured his imagination, the stories he spun with his words. How strange and precious life felt when he was around; now it seems a little dimmer without him.

It is a strange kind of silence that grows louder in her absence, a reminder that life continues to move, while I remain here, caught in the stillness of what once was.
